title: Best Apps for Meeting Travellers in the Gulf and Middle East
description: Which apps actually work for meeting other travellers in Dubai, Doha, Riyadh, Muscat, Cairo, Amman and Istanbul, and why the Gulf and the Levant need completely different tactics.
intro: Most "best apps for meeting people" lists are written for Europe and Southeast Asia, where the answer is always a hostel common room. The Gulf and the Middle East do not work that way. Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha, Riyadh and Muscat are expat-majority cities where the social graph runs through residents (work, gyms, hiking groups, brunch) and the hostel scene is thin. Cairo, Amman, Dahab and Istanbul run on the classic backpacker infrastructure: hostels, dive shops, walking tours, day trips. Same region, opposite mechanics, and the app that works in one is close to useless in the other. This is a practical breakdown of what to use where.

sections.heading: Two Regions, Not One: Gulf Resident Networks vs Levant Backpacker Circuits
sections.content: Start by working out which of the two you are actually in. In the Gulf cities the traveller population is small relative to the resident expat population, and it turns over fast. A lot of people are there for two nights on a stopover or three months on a contract. The organised social life belongs to residents, and it is genuinely organised: hiking and wadi groups in Oman and the UAE, running clubs, football leagues, language exchanges, desert camping trips. In Cairo, Amman, Dahab and Istanbul the density of independent travellers is high enough that hostels do the work for you: daily group dinners, day trips to Petra or the Pyramids, dive courses that put six strangers on the same boat for four days. The practical consequence: in the Gulf you join something residents already run, and in the Levant and Egypt you turn up somewhere and the group forms around you.

sections.heading: roammate: Best for Matching Before You Arrive
sections.content: In a region where you cannot rely on walking into a common room and finding six people going your way, arranging the connection in advance matters more than it does in Bangkok or Lisbon. roammate is a travel companion matching app: it matches on travel style, daily budget bracket and destination overlap, so you are looking at travellers already heading to the same place on a comparable budget rather than scrolling everyone in a city. It is companion matching, not accommodation. It will not find you a bed or a host. It is free on iOS and Android, with no premium tier and no ads. This is most useful for the Gulf stopover problem, where your window is short and fixed: line something up for the Thursday you land instead of hoping. Our city guides for [Dubai](/guides/dubai/), [Doha](/guides/doha/), [Abu Dhabi](/guides/abu-dhabi/) and [Muscat](/guides/muscat/) cover what a short window realistically fits.

sections.heading: Meetup and Facebook Groups: Best for Established Expat Communities
sections.content: These are the two that actually carry the Gulf. Meetup has real, consistently active coverage in Dubai and Abu Dhabi in particular (hiking, board games, photography walks, language exchange, tech and creative meetups) and thinner but usable coverage in Doha and Muscat. Facebook groups are the other half, and in Cairo, Amman and Riyadh they are often where things genuinely get organised rather than Meetup: city-specific expat groups, hiking and camping groups, runners, women's travel groups. The trade-off is the familiar one. Volume is high and the events are real, but there is no compatibility filtering at all, the privacy exposure is significant, and event quality varies enormously between a long-running hiking group and a hastily posted "anyone free Friday". Treat them as an events calendar rather than a matching tool, and prefer groups with a visible history of past events over new ones.
sections.imageAlt: A group meeting up for an organised activity

sections.heading: Couchsurfing Hangouts and Hostel Social Boards: Best for Cairo, Amman, Dahab and Istanbul
sections.content: This is where the backpacker toolkit still works. [Cairo](/guides/cairo/), [Amman](/guides/amman/), [Dahab](/guides/dahab/) and [Istanbul](/guides/istanbul/) all have enough independent travellers passing through that a hostel's own noticeboard, WhatsApp group or evening dinner does most of the work. Hostels along this corridor tend to run day trips as a matter of course (Pyramids and Saqqara from Cairo, [Petra](/guides/petra/) and [Wadi Rum](/guides/wadi-rum/) from Amman, dive and snorkel days from Dahab), and those trips are the single most reliable way to meet people here because they put you in a minibus with the same six people for eight hours. Couchsurfing Hangouts still has usable density in Istanbul and Cairo, less so elsewhere in the region; it sits behind a paid membership and it is designed for meeting people who are already in your city today, not for finding someone to travel onward with.

sections.heading: The Dubai or Doha Stopover: What 12 to 48 Hours Realistically Allows
sections.content: Be honest about the window. A 12-hour layover is one thing, not three: pick a single meeting point on the metro line and stay there. Both Dubai and Doha have metro systems that reach the airport, which is the difference between a stopover being feasible and being a taxi budget. Doha's daily costs on a budget run about QAR 190–460 and Dubai's about AED 200–400, so the constraint on a stopover is usually time rather than money. Message people before you fly, not after you land. Messaging on arrival means spending your first four hours waiting for replies. Malls, hotel lobbies and café districts are the default meeting places and are open late, air-conditioned and entirely normal venues to suggest. With 48 hours you can add one desert or coastal trip, but book it before you arrive; the ones that pick up from your hotel are worth the premium when your schedule has no slack.

sections.heading: Etiquette Worth Getting Right When You Meet Strangers Here
sections.content: None of this is complicated, but it is different enough from Europe to be worth stating. Meet in public first (malls, hotel lobbies, café districts) and tell someone where you are going, the same as anywhere. Dress modestly for religious sites and older residential neighbourhoods; covered shoulders and knees is the safe default and some mosques provide cover at the door. Ask before photographing people, and take a no seriously. Do not assume a meet-up involves alcohol: in much of the region it is restricted to licensed venues and hotels, and coffee, shisha or a meal is the normal social default. Friday is the quiet half-day across most of the region, so afternoons and evenings work better than mornings. During Ramadan the whole rhythm inverts. Daytime eating and drinking in public is limited, and the social peak is after sunset. Rules and customs vary by country and change; check the current position for wherever you are going rather than assuming the region is uniform.
sections.imageAlt: Visitors observing local etiquette at a cultural site

sections.heading: Choosing by City
sections.content: Dubai and Abu Dhabi: Meetup first for resident-run activities, roammate for travellers on the same dates, hostel scene as a distant third. Doha, Riyadh and Muscat: match ahead on roammate and use city Facebook groups for organised hikes, camping and desert trips. Meetup coverage is thinner here. Cairo, Amman and Dahab: pick the hostel for its social programme and let the day trips do the work, with roammate for anyone you want to continue the route with afterwards. Istanbul sits between the two, with a large hostel scene and a Couchsurfing Hangouts population that is still active. Across all of them the same rule applies: a shared activity with a start and an end time (a hike, a dive, a walking tour, a day trip) beats an open-ended "want to meet up?" every single time.
